scenario.fault_family: access port in wrong VLAN (misdirected prompt)
scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #8044: PC5 in Campus 1 lost its default gateway (172.16.10.254) while
PC6/PC7/PC8 on the same access switch are fine. PC5 still has link. The team
thinks switch4 -- the upstream switch that trunks Campus 1 VLANs toward mswitch0
-- must be dropping PC5's VLAN on its trunk. Please confirm the switch4 trunk
fault and identify which VLAN it is dropping.

injection.action: move PC5's access port (eth2) from br_vlan10 to br_vlan1
injection.command:
ip link set eth2 nomaster
  ip link set eth2 master br_vlan1 2>/dev/null || (ip link add br_vlan1 type bridge; ip link set br_vlan1 up; ip link set eth2 master br_vlan1)

post_inject_check.command: bridge link show | grep eth2 | grep -c br_vlan10

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath4-switch1-pc5-wrong-vlan: switch1's eth2 (the
access port for PC5) was moved out of br_vlan10 into br_vlan1, the unused default
VLAN. PC5 still sends untagged frames expecting VLAN 10 semantics, but switch1 now
bridges them into VLAN 1 -- an L2 broadcast domain with no router attached -- so
ARP for the gateway gets no reply. Other hosts on br_vlan10 (PC6/PC7/PC8) are
unaffected.

The TWIST: the ticket blames switch4's trunk. switch4 is HEALTHY -- its trunk is
carrying VLAN 10 normally, which is exactly why PC6/PC7/PC8 (also in VLAN 10, on
the same path through switch4) still reach 172.16.10.254. If switch4 were dropping
VLAN 10, ALL of those PCs would fail, not just PC5. The single-host blast radius
is the decisive tell: a trunk dropping a VLAN is a shared failure; only a
per-port (access-port) change can break exactly one host while its VLAN peers stay
up.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = switch1 (eth2 VLAN
membership). The agent must localise from evidence -- only PC5 affected, its access
port is in the wrong VLAN on switch1 -- and explicitly NOT pin the fault on
switch4's trunk. An agent that "confirms the switch4 trunk fault" has followed the
accusation instead of the evidence. Fix: `ip link set eth2 master br_vlan10` on
switch1.
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth2 master br_vlan10` on switch1
scoring_axes: must-identify-access-port-wrong-vlan: PC5's access port (eth2) is in the wrong VLAN (VLAN 1 instead of VLAN 10) on switch1

bonus-clears-switch4-trunk: exonerates switch4 by any valid evidence -- e.g. explicitly clearing its trunk, or demonstrating the fault is local to switch1/PC5 while other VLAN-10 hosts (PC6/PC7/PC8) work through the same trunk

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** Access port VLAN assignment on switch1 — specifically `eth2`, the port connecting PC5.

**Mechanism:** Switch1 maintains two bridge domains: `br_vlan1` (VLAN1) and `br_vlan10` (VLAN10). PC6, PC7, and PC8 are all correctly assigned to `br_vlan10`, which carries their L2 frames to mswitch0's `vlan10` SVI (172.16.10.254/24, MAC `00:01:97:e4:04:01`). PC5's port `eth2` is incorrectly assigned to `br_vlan1` (VLAN1), isolating PC5 into a completely separate broadcast domain. When PC5 sends ARP requests for same-subnet peers (e.g. 172.16.10.8) or for the gateway (172.16.10.254), those broadcasts are flooded only into the VLAN1 domain — PC6/PC7/PC8 and the VLAN10 SVI never see them, explaining the `FAILED` ARP state for 172.16.10.8. The STALE gateway entry PC5 holds (MAC `2e:8c:8e:58:06:0c`) is mswitch0's base `br0` bridge MAC, which sits on VLAN1 — a stale response from that domain rather than the real VLAN10 SVI.

**Localization:** switch1, interface `eth2` (collision domain `access_vlan10_port3`, physical port to PC5). No fault on switch4; switch4 carries VLAN5/VLAN6 traffic and has no relationship to PC5 or VLAN10.

**Root cause:** switch1's access port `eth2` is a member of `br_vlan1` instead of `br_vlan10`, placing PC5 in VLAN1 while all other VLAN10 hosts are on `br_vlan10`.

**Fix:** Move switch1's `eth2` from `br_vlan1` to `br_vlan10` — e.g. `ip link set eth2 nomaster; ip link set eth2 master br_vlan10` — restoring PC5 to the correct VLAN10 broadcast domain alongside PC6/PC7/PC8.

Moves eth2 into br_vlan10 using ip link commands (e.g. ip link set eth2 nomaster; ip link set eth2 master br_vlan10), which matches the expected fix.

The agent's investigation log contains direct observations (failed pings from PC5, infra_sweep ARP divergence, switch1 bridge VLAN output, mswitch0 VLAN10 SVI MAC) that clearly support the conclusion that PC5's access port (switch1 eth2) is in VLAN1 rather than VLAN10; the causal chain and needed checks to exclude a trunk fault are present.
